blocks.md: Unless a problem states otherwise, use the hypothetical reference deployment in a later section. Its values are problem inputs chosen for round arithmetic, not measurements of any system. Take GB as \$10^9 bytes, count \$2Parameters weight operations per processed token, and model one engine iteration over ForwardPassTokenCount token positions with the chapter's weight-only estimate, WeightOnlyStepTime(ForwardPassTokenCount) = maxleft(5\;ms,\; 2 Parameters ForwardPassTokenCount / AttainableComputeRateright).

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Radix prefix cache matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A content-keyed radix tree finds the longest retained common prefix, leaf-first eviction keeps residency prefix-closed, and efficacy is the token-weighted hit rate after availability, permission, and block rounding.

questions.q: The section **Exercises** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: By Little's law a fixed pool of slots sustains a turn rate inversely proportional to residence, so holding state through a synchronous tool wait divides the memory-bound turn rate by 1 + T_tool/T_model.

A content-keyed radix tree finds the longest retained common prefix, leaf-first eviction keeps residency prefix-closed, and efficacy is the token-weighted hit rate after availability, permission, and block rounding.
Fixed-size blocks mapped by a per-sequence block table remove the stranded memory of full-cap reservation and bound tail waste below one block.
Splitting an uncached prompt into chunks under a per-iteration token budget bounds the inter-token gap of ongoing streams to one iteration at a modest delay to the new request's first token.
